source.title_on_document: Navigating the Jagged Technological Frontier: Field Experimental Evidence of the Effects of AI on Knowledge Worker Productivity and Quality

supplement.where: Appendices A-E at the end of this PDF (PDF pp. 44-58), which the main text cites (for example 'For a detailed analysis, refer to Appendix D', PDF p. 16). No separate or online supplement is mentioned. The pre-registration (osf.io/ytaev) is embargoed and 'available from the authors upon request' (PDF p. 9, fn. 2).
supplement.holds: A: task texts (PDF pp. 44-46). B: recommendation-quality rubric (PDF pp. 46-48). C: retainment of GPT-4 text among AI users (PDF pp. 49-51). D: the definition of the similarity measure, the simulated ChatGPT-only condition, and the only statement of the idea-list creativity result (PDF pp. 52-54). E: qualitative Centaur and Cyborg typology (PDF pp. 55-58). No appendix prints means, standard errors, or tests for the similarity or idea-list creativity results. Appendix D says the creativity ratings are presented 'in Table 1', but neither of the two tables numbered 1 in the PDF holds them: the main-text Table 1 is the quality regression table (PDF p. 38), and Appendix E's Table 1 lists Centaur and Cyborg practices (PDF p. 56).

paper_design_summary: Of 852 Boston Consulting Group consultants who answered the enrollment survey, 758 completed and were analyzed in two separate experiments. In each, they first did a baseline task without AI and were then randomly assigned to no AI, GPT-4 access (GPT Only), or GPT-4 plus a prompt-engineering overview (GPT + Overview). In the inside-the-frontier experiment (385 consultants analyzed), they developed a new shoe product over 18 questions; human graders and GPT-4 scored every answer, the question-1 idea lists received a 1-10 creativity rating from a rater the paper does not name, and Universal Sentence Encoder similarity was computed across subjects' shoe ideas. In the outside-the-frontier experiment (373 analyzed), they wrote a brand recommendation from data and interviews, scored for correctness and, on a 1-10 rubric, for the quality of the tactical actions they proposed.

studies.label: Inside-the-frontier experiment (creative product innovation: new shoe concept, 18 questions)

assignment.what_was_assigned: Access to GPT-4 for the experimental task: none (Control), GPT Only, or GPT + Overview (GPT-4 plus a prompt-engineering overview). All participants first did an assessment task without AI. Assignment was stratified on gender, location, tenure at BCG, openness to innovation, and native English status.
assignment.quote: Following this, participants were randomly assigned to one of three conditions to assess the influence of AI on their tasks, with these conditions being consistent across both experiments.

participants.exclusions: Of 852 consultants who answered the enrollment survey, 758 (about 89 percent) completed the experiment (PDF p. 9, fn. 3); 385 of them were in this experiment. The paper does not say whether the 94 non-completers had been randomized, or to which experiment or arm, so no count at randomization is recorded. Per-arm counts are not reported. Tables 1-3 report 385 observations. The number of subjects in the similarity analysis is not stated.
participants.who: Individual-contributor strategy consultants at Boston Consulting Group. The paper gives a share of the firm's individual-contributor consultants, about 7 percent, only for all 758 completers of both experiments; it gives no share for this experiment alone.
participants.country: Multinational (BCG offices around the world); no country breakdown given
participants.quote: Approximately half of the participants (385 consultants) tackled a series of tasks where they were prompted to conceptualize and develop new product ideas, focusing on aspects such as creativity, analytical skills, persuasiveness and writing skills.
participants.locator: PDF p. 10 (printed p. 6), Section 2; Table 1, PDF p. 38 (printed p. 34), Observations 385

ai_tool.name_model: OpenAI GPT-4 as available at the end of April 2023, default system prompt and temperature, through a company platform built on the OpenAI API that mirrors ChatGPT
ai_tool.how_used: Free interactive chat with GPT-4 during the 90-minute experimental task; all prompts and responses were logged (PDF p. 12). Appendix C reports high retainment of GPT-4 text in submitted answers, with a mode of average retainment of about 0.87 (PDF p. 50).

task.description: Develop a new shoe for an underserved market or sport over 18 questions (Appendix A, PDF pp. 45-46): at least 10 ideas, pick the best, describe a prototype, list launch steps, name it, segment the market, choose and assess segments, write slogans and ways to test them, a 500-word memo, a focus-group plan and questions, a competitor list, an inspirational memo, a press release, and an outline for an HBR-style article. Baseline (assessment) task: the first five of these questions for a new drink, without AI.
task.duration: Assessment task 30 minutes; experimental task 90 minutes, and participants had to stay on the task page for the full time (PDF p. 11)

outcomes.name: Quality: composite human-graded score across the 18 questions
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Each answered question was graded by two human graders 'from BCG, or MBA students at a top program' (PDF p. 13, fn. 6); question score = mean of the two grades; composite 'Quality' = mean over the 18 questions. The paper does not state the composite's scale: Figure 2 plots it on an axis running from 1 to 8 (PDF p. 32), and Figure 5's notes give 'average scores (on a 1-10 scale)' without naming the grader or the measure (PDF p. 35). The questions span creativity, analytical thinking, writing, and persuasiveness (PDF p. 13), so the composite measures overall task quality, not creativity alone. Variants: Table 1 cols (2)-(3) add the assessment-task score and demographics, and col (3) adds AI-familiarity controls. Robustness: per-question regressions with the two AI arms merged (18 questions x 3 specifications with human grades = 54 regressions, Figure 3, PDF p. 33) all show significant effects; mean effect 1.69, 'a 46.6% increase over the control mean' (PDF p. 14). Figure 3 does not say which line is which question, so no question-level estimate (for example question 1, the shoe ideas) can be read.

outcomes.name: Creativity rating (1-10) of each subject's question-1 shoe idea list
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Appendix D: 'We obtained evaluations of each subject's idea list along the dimension of creativity, ranging from 1 to 10' (PDF p. 53). No passage says who or what produced these evaluations, so the measure is coded not_stated, the code other forms use for an unstated scorer (the form-spec measure list has none). Two readings remain. (1) The main-text human graders, 'from BCG, or MBA students at a top program' (PDF p. 13, fn. 6), which would be expert_raters. (2) GPT-4, which would be automated_score. Appendix C uses the same wording for its 1-10 answer evaluations, plots them on a 'Footwear Average Score' axis with ticks at 7, 8, and 9, and reports an intercept of about 7.55 (PDF p. 51, Figure 3); that range matches the GPT-graded scale (Table 1 control mean 7.207), not the human-graded one (4.099). No table in the PDF holds these results: the PDF's two tables numbered 1 are the main-text quality table (PDF p. 38) and Appendix E's practices table (PDF p. 56). The two AI arms are not separated in the text.

outcomes.name: Between-subject semantic similarity of question-1 shoe ideas (Universal Sentence Encoder)
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: Each of a subject's roughly 10 question-1 ideas is encoded with Google's Universal Sentence Encoder (512 dimensions). Each idea's average inner product with all ideas of other subjects in the same condition is averaged over the subject's ideas to give a subject-level 'between semantic similarity' (PDF p. 52). Higher similarity means less variation, so the sign is reversed relative to diversity. Only question 1 is analyzed.

contrasts.reported: Density plot by condition with each condition's mean as a dashed vertical line; no means, SEs, or tests printed. The GPT Only mean line lies to the right of (above) the Control line: similarity higher, diversity lower (sign reversed). Text: 'there is a marked reduction in the variability of these ideas compared to those not using AI.'

diversity_detail.metric: Subject-level mean inner product (semantic similarity) between each of the subject's ideas and all ideas of other subjects in the same condition
diversity_detail.computed_over: Each idea against all ideas of other subjects within the same experimental condition, averaged over the subject's roughly 10 ideas
diversity_detail.uncertainty: None reported: density plots with condition means as dashed vertical lines; no standard error, interval, or test
diversity_detail.notes: Figure 6 (PDF p. 36) and Appendix D Figure 1 (PDF p. 53) show the same plot. Mean lines from lowest to highest similarity: Control, GPT + Overview, GPT Only, GPT No Humans; no values are printed. Figure 6 notes call the measure 'Average Within-Subject Semantic Similarity', while Appendix D defines it as between-subject similarity. Appendix D Figure 1 labels the arms Group A (Access to ChatGPT), Group B (Access to ChatGPT + Training), and Group C (No access to ChatGPT). Appendix D's text has a typo ('subjects without access to ChatGPT tend to produce ideas with less semantic similarity (more conceptual variation) than those without access'). The number of subjects or ideas in the analysis is not stated.

outcomes.name: Between-subject semantic similarity: simulated ChatGPT-only answers ('GPT No Humans') versus the human arms
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: The question-1 prompt was given to ChatGPT in 100 independent sessions, 'each meant to represent a separate GPT Only subject', and the same between semantic similarity was computed within this simulated condition (PDF p. 52). No person produced the simulated answers. Of the human arms, only Control wrote without AI; GPT Only and GPT + Overview subjects wrote their ideas with GPT-4 (PDF p. 12). So only the contrast with Control compares AI output with human output in the sense of codebook section 3, and the contrast with the two AI arms compares AI-only output with output that people wrote with GPT-4. The record keeps the two contrasts apart. Appendix D calls the simulated condition 'GPT Only', the label of a human arm in the main text; Figure 6 calls it 'GPT No Humans'. Unit coded output: one simulated session's idea list, not a person.

contrasts.treatment_arm: GPT No Humans (100 simulated ChatGPT sessions)
contrasts.reported: Appendix D: 'We also observe that the GPT Only group has the highest degree of between semantic similarity, measured across each of the simulated subjects.' In Figure 6 the GPT No Humans mean line lies to the right of (above) the Control line: similarity higher, diversity lower (sign reversed). No numbers printed.

studies.label: Outside-the-frontier experiment (business case: brand recommendation note)

assignment.what_was_assigned: The same three conditions as S1 (Control, GPT Only, GPT + Overview), after an assessment task done without AI.
assignment.quote: Following this, participants were randomly assigned to one of three conditions to assess the influence of AI on their tasks, with these conditions being consistent across both experiments.

arms.name: GPT + Overview
arms.description: GPT-4 chat tool plus the prompt-engineering overview.

participants.exclusions: 373 consultants analyzed in this experiment (see S1 for the 852 to 758 attrition). Tables 4-5 report 373 observations; Table 6 (recommendation quality) reports 372, split 105 incorrect and 267 correct in cols (3)-(4). Per-arm counts are not reported.
participants.quote: The other half (373 consultants) engaged in business problem-solving tasks using quantitative data, customer and company interviews, and including a persuasive writing component.
participants.locator: PDF p. 10 (printed p. 6), Section 2; Tables 4-6, PDF pp. 41-43

ai_tool.name_model: OpenAI GPT-4 as available at the end of April 2023, default system prompt and temperature
ai_tool.how_used: ChatGPT-like chat during the 60-minute experimental task.

task.description: Write a 500-750 word note to the CEO of a hypothetical company (Kleding): pick one of three brands to invest in, support the choice with data and interview quotations, and 'suggest innovative and tactical actions the CEO can take to improve this chosen brand' (Appendix A, PDF pp. 44-45). The brand choice has a correct answer, and the task was designed so that GPT-4 would err (PDF p. 12). The recommendation-quality rubric scores only the proposed tactical actions, not the brand choice (Appendix B, PDF pp. 47-48). Baseline task: the same format for distribution channels, without AI.
task.duration: Assessment and experimental tasks 60 minutes each; participants could finish early (PDF p. 11)

outcomes.name: Recommendation quality (1-10 rubric score of the proposed tactical actions)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Scored 1-10 'by two different sets of human graders (one of BCG consultants not involved in the experiment, and the other of business school students with grading experience)' with the authors' rubric (PDF p. 19; Appendix B, PDF pp. 46-48). The rubric scores only the tactical actions that the note proposes: whether they are identified, aligned with strategy, described in implementable detail, backed by business reasoning, and tied to an impact on profit. It has no novelty or creativity criterion and does not score the brand choice, and the paper reports the AI effect 'regardless of the correctness of their answer' (PDF p. 19). The task asks for 'innovative and tactical actions' and says 'Please be creative' (PDF p. 45). Coded with_ai under the codebook rule (AI available, construct not diversity): the scored output is business ideas with more than one acceptable answer, judged on usefulness (codebook section 1). The reconciliation had coded none; Review 1 may still treat the brand case as out of scope. Variants: col (2) adds the assessment-task score and controls. Cols (3)-(4) rerun col (2) on subjects with incorrect (105) and correct (267) brand choices: col (3) GPT + Overview 1.343* (0.725), GPT Only 1.570* (0.807), control mean 5.325, F-test p 0.664; col (4) GPT + Overview 1.544*** (0.253), GPT Only 0.841*** (0.285), control mean 5.954, F-test p 0.011 (Table 6, PDF p. 43). Figure 8 pools the two AI arms ('Test Group'): correct answers 5.95 (control) vs 7.21, '+21%'; incorrect answers 5.33 vs 6.28, '+18%' (PDF p. 37).

contrasts.reported: Table 6 col (1): GPT Only 1.046*** (0.289); col (2): 0.941*** (0.265). Control Mean 5.856; Observations 372; robust standard errors. Text: 'GPT Only increases the score by 1.05 (17.9% over the control mean)'.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 43 (printed p. 39), Table 6; PDF p. 19 (printed p. 15)

Funding came in part from Harvard Business School.

eligibility.reason: S1 randomly assigned individual consultants (stratified) to GPT-4 access (two arms) or no AI on a product-innovation task, with 385 people analyzed, far above 50; per-arm counts are not reported. Outcomes are scored on their output while AI was available: the human-graded composite quality (Table 1), a 1-10 creativity rating of the idea lists by a rater the paper does not name (Appendix D, text only), and Universal Sentence Encoder similarity across subjects' ideas (Figure 6, figure only). The creativity-specific results have no printed statistics in this working paper. S2 also meets all three criteria: the same random assignment, 373 people analyzed (372 for this outcome), and a human-graded 1-10 rubric score of the tactical business actions that the note had to propose, produced with GPT-4 available (Table 6) and coded with_ai under the codebook rule. Its primary outcome, correctness of the brand choice, answers none of the three questions. S1 qualifies whether or not Review 1 keeps S2 in scope.

one_line_finding: Among 385 BCG consultants analyzed in the shoe-product experiment, GPT-4 access raised the human-graded composite quality score by 1.556 (SE 0.080, GPT Only) and 1.746 (SE 0.074, GPT + Overview) over a control mean of 4.099 (PDF p. 38, Table 1), while the across-subject similarity of their shoe ideas was higher in both AI arms than in the control arm, shown only as density plots with no statistics (PDF p. 36, Figure 6).
open_questions: The file is the September 2023 working paper. Does the Organization Science (2026) version of record, or an online supplement to it, print numbers (means, SEs, tests) for the similarity and idea-list creativity results, or drop them? No similarity contrast has a printed statistic, GPT + Overview versus GPT Only included.

Who or what rated the idea-list creativity in Appendix D: the BCG or MBA human graders (expert_raters), or GPT-4 (automated_score)? The final form codes S1-O3's measure not_stated. Appendix C uses the same wording for its 1-10 evaluations and plots them on a 7-9 axis (PDF p. 51), the range of the GPT-graded scale; the cited Table 1 is not in the PDF.
Per-arm counts are not reported. Were the 94 enrollees who did not complete (852 to 758) already randomized, and how many subjects and ideas enter the similarity analysis?
Graders were from BCG or MBA students at a top program; coded expert_raters. Review 1 may prefer human_raters for the MBA students.

S2 recommendation quality is coded with_ai in the final form, because its rubric scores only the tactical actions that the task asks to be 'innovative' and 'creative'. Review 1 may decide that the brand case is an analytic task outside the section's scope, which would recode it none and leave S1 as the only core sample. S1 meets all three criteria either way.
notes: PDF page numbers are the file's page numbers; main-text printed page n sits on PDF page n + 4 (Table 1 is printed p. 34, PDF p. 38). The markdown file on disk covers the whole document, Tables 1-6 and Appendices A-E included (markdown lines 585-1055); both screeners wrote that it stops at Table 1, which does not hold for the current file. Every number recorded here was checked against the PDF page. Outcomes not listed because they bear on none of the three questions and neither screener listed them: S1 percent of questions completed (Table 2, PDF p. 39: GPT + Overview 0.111*** (0.020), GPT Only 0.090*** (0.021), control mean 0.824) and time to reach the last question (Table 3, PDF p. 40); S2 timing (Table 5, PDF p. 42). Appendix C (retainment of GPT-4 text) covers AI users only and is descriptive. Appendix E (Centaur and Cyborg practices) is qualitative and describes '244 professional consultants' on the analytic task (PDF p. 55). In each experiment the two AI arms share one control group; under codebook rule 8.3 the GPT Only arm is closest to free use of a general chatbot. The final form codes S2 recommendation quality with_ai, so S2 is a second with_ai sample (see final.challenge_resolution).

open_items.item: Version of record: the file is the September 2023 working paper. Whether the Organization Science (2026) article, or a supplement to it, prints means, standard errors, or tests for the Figure 6 similarity contrasts (GPT + Overview vs GPT Only included) and the Appendix D creativity ratings, or drops these results (open question 1). The across_people records stay figure-only until then.

Who or what rated the Appendix D idea-list creativity: the BCG or MBA graders (expert_raters) or GPT-4 (automated_score). S1-O3's measure is coded not_stated (open question 2 and the one unresolved reconciliation difference). The cited Table 1 is not in this PDF; if the journal version does not say, the authors.

Per-arm counts are printed for neither experiment, the paper does not say whether the 94 enrollees who did not complete (852 to 758) had been randomized, and the number of subjects and ideas in the similarity analysis is not stated (open question 3). Criterion 2 rests on 385 people analyzed in S1 and does not need them. If the journal version does not print them, the authors.

Grader code: the graders were from BCG or MBA students at a top program (S1) and BCG consultants or business-school students (S2), coded expert_raters; Review 1 may prefer human_raters for the students (open question 4).

Scope of S2: recommendation quality is now coded with_ai, because its rubric scores the tactical actions that the task asks to be innovative and creative. Review 1 may treat the brand case as an analytic task outside the section, which would recode it none (open question 5). S1 meets all three criteria either way, so only S2's place as a second core sample depends on it.
